title: Correspondences
text:
Nature is a temple where living pillars

Sometimes let confused words spring forth;

Man passes through forests of symbols

That observe him with familiar glances.


Like prolonged echoes that from afar blend

In a dark and deep unity,

Vast as night and as clarity,

Perfumes, colors, and sounds respond to one another.


There are perfumes fresh as children's flesh,

Soft as oboes, green as meadows,

And others, corrupted, rich, and triumphant,


That have the expansion of infinite things,

Like amber, musk, benzoin, and incense,

That sing the transports of spirit and senses.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the synesthetic doctrine of perfumes, colors, and sounds answering one another.

title: The Cracked Bell
text:
On winter nights it is bitter and sweet

To listen, beside the fire that throbs and smokes,

As distant memories rise very slowly

To the sound of carillons ringing in the mist.


Happy the bell with energetic throat

That, despite its age, preserved and alert,

Faithfully casts out its religious cry

Like an old soldier keeping watch in his tent!


But my soul is cracked, and when, in its weariness,

It wants to people the nocturnal cold with songs,

It often happens that its tired voice


Resembles the death rattle of a forgotten wounded man

Beside a lake of blood, beneath a heap of dead,

Who expires, motionless, amid immense efforts.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the contrast between the faithful bell and the speaker's cracked, dying voice.

title: The Old Woman's Despair
text:
The little wrinkled old woman felt full of delight on seeing the pretty creature celebrated by everyone, whom everyone wanted to please; that pretty being as fragile as she, the little old woman, and like her also without teeth or hair.


And she approached to make caresses and pleasant gestures to it.


But the child, terrified, struggled as the poor decrepit woman caressed him, filling the house with his howls.


Then the little old woman withdrew into her eternal solitude, and wept in a corner, saying: "Ah! For us, unfortunate old females, the time has passed for pleasing even the innocent; and we even cause horror to small children when we go to give them affection!"
editorial_note: The translation preserves the prose poem's cruel reversal between infant fragility and the old woman's rejected tenderness.

title: The Death of the Poor
text:
It is Death that consoles, ah! and makes one live;

It is the object of life, and it is the only hope

That, like an elixir, sustains and intoxicates us,

and gives us courage to advance to the end;


Through storm, and snow, and frost,

It is the vibrating clarity on our black horizon,

It is the famous lodging inscribed in the book,

Where one will be able to eat, and sleep, and sit;


It is an Angel who holds between magnetic fingers

Sleep and the gift of ecstatic dreams,

And remakes the bed of poor and naked people;


It is the glory of the Gods, it is the mystic granary,

It is the poor man's purse and his old homeland,

It is the portico opened onto unknown Heavens!
editorial_note: The translation keeps Death as consolation, shelter, granary, purse, homeland, and opened gate.

title: II               The Albatross
text:
Calm yourself, my pain, and make your anguish serene.

You longed for night. It is descending now. Here it is.

A dark

atmosphere covers Paris. It will bring

peace to a few, sorrow to many others.

While the

crowd that surrenders to pleasure,

Its merciless executioner, longs through the streets

To hunt

remorse beneath the sleepless feast,

You, pain, come to me. Give me your hand when you see

That it is possible

to escape the years already dead

With their old suits on the celestial balcony.

Disappointments already sprout, as they

come out of the sea,

When the sun, beneath an arch, dies in the distance.

Now,

like a shroud descending from the east,

Observe, my pain: the immense night advances.

Version by

José Emilio Pacheco
editorial_note: This mislabeled catalog record keeps the Albatross title while translating the Recueillement text and attribution present in the source.
